title: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages
answer: Picture a middle school class studying the abolition movement. The teacher sets up an AI tool to answer questions in the voice of Frederick Douglass, and students line up to interview him.

papers.title: What message features influence the intention to share misinformation about COVID-19 on social media? The role of efficacy and novelty
papers.finding: Korean experiment (N=1,012) on how novelty and efficacy of misinformation affect sharing through emotion and credibility.

papers.title: Who spread COVID-19 (mis)information online? Differential informedness, psychological mechanisms, and intervention strategies
papers.finding: Chinese surveys: misinformed and uninformed people were more likely to spread misinformation; positive-emotion content spread more.

papers.why: Supports teaching students to seek news actively rather than rely on feeds or AI summaries.
papers.title: Social media may hinder learning about science; social media's role in learning about COVID-19
papers.finding: US two-wave panel. Getting news from social media fostered a news-finds-me belief, which left people less informed and more misinformed about COVID-19.

children.name: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
children.blurb: Coaching students through primary sources means using a school configured AI tool as a question asking coach rather than as an interpreter of the material.

children.name: Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation
children.blurb: Historical role play, labeled as simulation, lets students interview or question a program that imagines a historical figure, a delegate at a constitutional convention, or a witness to an event.

children.name: Perspectives and Missing Voices
children.blurb: Perspectives and Missing Voices is a social studies use of AI in which a tool helps students compare how different people might describe the same event and helps teachers find groups that textbooks often leave out.

children.name: Why a Teacher Reads First
children.blurb: Every AI tool that produces perspectives, summaries, or historical content should be read by a teacher before students see it.

children.name: Current Events and Misinformation
children.blurb: The idea of current events and misinformation is about using AI to help prepare leveled news discussions while teaching students to verify what they see.

children.name: Civic Simulations, Debate, and Mock Trial
children.blurb: Civic simulations, debate, and mock trial let students practice civics rather than only read about it.

children.name: Timelines, Maps, and Local History
children.blurb: This idea uses visual tools like timelines and maps, plus local history interviews, to help students understand sequence, place, and community.

children.name: World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment
children.blurb: This idea is that AI can add world language practice when human practice partners are scarce, while teachers keep judgment over feedback and grades.

children.name: Translation as a Lesson
children.blurb: Translation as a Lesson is a translation critique exercise in which students translate a passage themselves and then compare their version with one from Microsoft Translator, identifying where the machine got the meaning right, where it lost tone or idiom, and where it made outright errors.

children.name: Access for Every Student
children.blurb: Access for Every Student means using AI to make social studies, civics, and world languages content readable and understandable for all learners without lowering the intellectual demand.

children.name: Heritage Speakers and Family Languages
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI to support students who speak a language other than English at home, especially when their speaking and listening are stronger than their reading and writing.

children.name: Geography and Data
children.blurb: Geography and data can be combined in social studies so students examine population, climate, or trade information for regions and identify patterns.

children.name: Planning and Assessment in These Subjects
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI to draft planning and assessment materials in social studies, civics, and world languages, then having the teacher review and edit them.

sections.body: This part of school life is social studies, civics, and world languages, where AI can answer questions in the voice of a historical figure, show how different people might see the same event, give a language learner endless conversation practice, and let a class explore economic or political choices through simulation. The book says these are powerful uses, but it also says AI tools produce fluent text that can include invented quotes, dates, and sources. In most subjects an invented detail is a mistake to correct, but in history and civics an invented quote attributed to a real person can distort the past and mislead students about what people actually believed. The chapter covers primary source coaching, historical role play, perspective taking and missing voices, current events and misinformation, civic simulations and debate, timelines and local history, and several uses in world languages. A section on bias explains why every perspective tool needs a teacher reading first, and Figure 9.2 maps the ideas and their evidence.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works is the power of AI to show multiple perspectives, provide endless conversation practice, and support simulations, but the book holds that these uses depend on a teacher reading what the tool says before students rely on it. What does not work is the convincing simulation, where a class interviews a simulated historical figure, students copy memorable quotes into essays, nobody checks whether the figure ever said them, and the invented history spreads. The book says a general policy on AI use is not enough on its own, and that only one idea in this chapter carries strong evidence, so most should begin as small pilots. The rule it holds to is a simple review practice that teachers actually follow: any AI generated historical content, perspective, or source is read by the teacher before students use it, simulations are labeled, and quotes are verified against real sources. The Thirty Day Move is to adopt the simulation rules in Figure 9.3 and the teacher check in Figure 9.4 for every social studies and world language class, share them in a short meeting with an example of an invented quote, and run one misinformation lab in at least one grade using Figure 9.5.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A teacher planning source work would go to Coaching Students Through Primary Sources, then to Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation, and to Perspectives and Missing Voices, with Why a Teacher Reads First as the rule that ties them together. For current events and civic action, Current Events and Misinformation and Civic Simulations, Debate, and Mock Trial connect to the research the site holds, including What message features influence the intention to share misinformation about COVID-19 on social media? The role of efficacy and novelty, Who spread COVID-19 (mis)information online? Differential informedness, psychological mechanisms, and intervention strategies, and Social media may hinder learning about science; social media's role in learning about COVID-19. A teacher working with time and place would use Timelines, Maps, and Local History and Geography and Data. For language learning, World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment, Translation as a Lesson, Access for Every Student, and Heritage Speakers and Family Languages cover practice, judgment, translation, access, and family languages, and a parent would go to Access for Every Student and Heritage Speakers and Family Languages to see how their child's language and access are supported. Leaders and teachers would go to Planning and Assessment in These Subjects to fit this work into planning and assessment.
